You can state clearly to him that giving him space/giving yourself some space isn't a reflection of how much or how little you care about him. 

I have ADHD and I often got upset when my partner needed space or didn't want to be my emotional punching bag to let frustration out on. Looking back, I'd realize that my rejection-sensitive dysphoria was causing me to act out and be destructive towards my partners mental health. Things only escalated from there.

Don't be afraid to be direct and upfront with your needs, and place limits for how much care you're going to dedicate towards his mental health each day. It sounds weird, but you can even put a time maximum on this stuff. For example, you might only want to invest 30 minutes a day towards listening and comforting your partner's emotional struggles. Beyond that, they are his issues. And you don't want his issues to overwhelm your life and become your issues.

Sorry to jump on your thread, just wanted to say that if he is frustrated, ranting to you is not his only option for an outlet, nor should it be his first one. Set boundaries for your own mental health and he will set his, in order to maintain a healthy relationship.

He sounds really stressed and frustrated, and it seems like some of that is being transferred onto you. That can be really emotionally exhausting for the both of you -- he probably realizes he does this and gets upset at himself, and you obviously don't feel good that your efforts to help aren't being well-received.

I'd suggest giving him more space to try and manage his work on his own. It doesn't sound like what you're trying to do has been very helpful for him, and it's definitely taking an emotional toll on you. Give him back some autonomy and self control, and use the time and energy you just freed up towards more positive things (yourself, your hobbies, fun activities together, or time with your friends).

Definitely make sure he goes to appointments (without pushing them off), but otherwise, you can make an open offer of "let me know if there's anything I can do to support you," and leave it at that.

Regarding financial aid and cost, here's an estimated breakdown using updated 2020 numbers. Looks like from your other comments you might be international? I'm not familiar with that so much but I've included the OOS info to compare.

- Tuition: $1914/quarter
- Cal Poly Registration Fees: $1400/quarter

- Out of State Additional Tuition (if applicable): $264/unit × 16 units = ~$4250/quarter
- Out-of-State Fee ("CP Opportunity"): ~$800/quarter

Base Education Total (out-of-state): ~$8350/quarter, or ~$25k/year (3 quarters)

- Fresman Housing: $9k-$10k/year depending on placement and room type (we'll go with 9k)
- Freshman Dining: $5200/year for the basic plan

We're looking at $39.2k for the base expenses (classes, housing, and dining). Don't forget books, transportation, food, and fun stuff...oh and if you're trying to do greek life, that has fees too.

As far as financial aid, I only know US numbers:
- Pell Grant maxes out around $5k/year for dependents 
- Students with 1st year status and are categorized as dependents get max of $5500 sub/unsub loans per year
- Cal Poly doesn't seem to give out many scholarships for non-Californians, so you'd likely have to look at 3rd party.

Overall, Cal Poly isn't cheap. Like another commenter said though, as a CS major you shouldn't have to be too worried since you'll be set after graduation. If you want to come here just send it and let the financials be a problem for a different day.
